query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The quality and integrity of the native oxide film on pre-exposed Q235 steel governs its corrosion behavior in harsh environments. In chloride-rich media and at elevated temperatures, microstructural defects (such as cracks or spalls) in the naturally formed oxide film allow aggressive attack and pitting; conversely, maintaining or even modestly enhancing the film’s integrity should suppress such corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Commercial Q235 steel in its as-received, pre-exposure state with its naturally developed native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Three sample groups: (1) untreated Q235 steel (intact native oxide), (2) Q235 steel with a deliberately mechanically disrupted oxide (to simulate compromised protection), and (3) Q235 steel with an enhanced oxide layer prepared via mild anodic oxidation to promote a thicker, more adherent passivating film.
generation.conditions: Controlled immersion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution conducted at room temperature (~25°C) and at an elevated temperature (60°C). Tests run for durations up to 72 hours under static conditions with periodic electrochemical and microscopic measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: The physical integrity and microstructure (continuity, thickness, composition) of the native/passivating oxide film on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: In aggressive environments, chloride ions and elevated thermal energy accelerate the breakdown of a compromised oxide film via localized dissolution, cracking, and spallation, which lead to pitting and accelerated corrosion. A robust, intact or enhanced oxide film acts as a protective barrier that suppresses these localized degradation processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated reference, samples with a disrupted oxide layer will exhibit higher corrosion current densities, lower impedance, visible pitting, and greater weight loss, especially at 60°C. Conversely, samples with an enhanced oxide film will show lower corrosion current densities, higher impedance, and fewer pitting sites than the untreated state.
generation.baseline: Pre-exposed as-received Q235 steel with its native oxide film, tested in a mild environment (room temperature, absence of aggressive chloride disruption).
generation.boundary: The study is limited to variations in the native oxide film state of commercial Q235 steel under immersion in up to 3.5% NaCl solution and temperature conditions from 25°C to 60°C. It does not account for alloy modifications, mechanical loading, or environmental extremes beyond these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in the native oxide film composition and microstructural heterogeneities among commercial Q235 steel samples may affect the absolute corrosion rates. The quantitative differences in electrochemical metrics and morphological changes could be sensitive to slight variations in processing and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Q235 steel samples as described: (1) as-received (intact oxide), (2) mechanically abraded to disrupt the oxide, and (3) mildly anodized to enhance the oxide film. Immerse specimens in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at both 25°C and 60°C for 24, 48, and 72 hours. Use electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization to assess corrosion behavior, complemented by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology and weight loss measurements.
measurements: Corrosion current density from polarization curves
Surface morphology and pitting density via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the electrochemical and morphological data show no significant differences between the three groups (i.e., neither the disrupted nor the enhanced oxide treatments yield statistically different corrosion indicators compared to the untreated reference) or if the enhanced oxide group does not exhibit lower corrosion rates and fewer pitting sites in both temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that the integrity of the native oxide film governs corrosion onset/suppression in Q235 steel will be falsified.
